persons.name: John Dean Caton

occupation.note: One of the six lawyers Andreas counts in the town at the close of 1833, and its corporation counsel: 'On December 4, George W. Snow became Assessor and Surveyor, and John Dean Caton, Corporation Counsel.'

persons.note: ARRIVED 19 JUNE 1833 - A DAY-PRECISE ARRIVAL, which only four households in this parcel have. Andreas: 'The first lawyer in Chicago to make a living by his profession alone was Giles Spring; and separated from him by a few days was John Dean Caton, who arrived June 19, 1833.' Early in July the two of them kept office 'as was facetiously said, "On the head of a barrel at the corner of Lake and Wells"', and in December 1833 Caton rented from Dr Temple 'the back room and attic of his "building" on Lake Street, converting the attic into a bedroom, and extending to Spring the courtesy of desk-room in the room below, which thus became the first law-office in Chicago'. In August 1833 he defended six or seven free coloured men before the Court of County Commissioners and obtained certificates of freedom for them, his fee a dollar from each. OLD SETTLERS, 1882 — CORROBORATION, NOT A NEW FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's fourth annual reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, held 18 May 1882, printed this man among the guests present as “Caton, John Dean, 1900 Calumet avenue, Chicago.” (Chicago Tribune, 19 May 1882). The club's criterion was residence in Chicago before 1 January 1840 and majority by then: the roster therefore corroborates a pre-1840 Chicago residence and says he was alive in 1882. It gives NO year of arrival, and the address it prints is where he lived in 1882, forty-seven years after the scene date — it is not an 1835 residence and is not read as one. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 2 times: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Caton, John Dean” (tax_1833_015, line 67); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Caton, John Dean” (poll_1834_025, line 194). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Caton' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

research_note: THE FIRST LAW OFFICE IN CHICAGO WAS AN ATTIC A MAN SLEPT IN, and that is the most useful thing this household contributes: a documented example of the live-above-the-shop pattern that the inferred phase will have to assume for most of the town's tradesmen. SIX LAWYERS ARE DOCUMENTED IN THE 1833 TOWN and this parcel writes five as households - Heacock, Hamilton, Caton, Spring, Fullerton and Casey being the six; all are written. Not one of their offices is a structure record.

address_later.note: Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints this address against this person, in the entry quoted on the card: 'Caton, John I)., attorney at law, Clark street'. It is evidence about 1839, written here as 1839's and read back onto no 1835 claim. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. The value is the volume's own line, split by its crosswalk on the entry's punctuation. These volumes set the trade first and its qualifiers after it on the same line, so the split may carry an employer, a market or a corner along with the trade. The printed entry is quoted beside the value for exactly that reason: the split is checkable against it, and neither is read into an 1835 claim.
